title: All created things (277–279)
hookLine: all created things pass, all are painful, all forms are without self; seeing this, one turns from suffering

lines: NOTHING IN THE ROOM HOLDS STILL.
cards: Look around the room you're in. The coffee going cold. The phone battery a little lower than an hour ago.
The light through the window at a different angle than this morning. The plant that has grown a leaf you haven't noticed. Your own body, a few more cells replaced since you woke up.
Nothing in the room is holding still. Not one thing. Everyone knows this, and still plans as if the world were a photograph.
Chapter twenty holds three short verses, all built alike, that say so.

teach.b: The three verses share one shape. Each names something true of everything, then says the one who knows and sees it grows weary of suffering and turns from it: "this is the way to purity."
Verse two seventy-seven, in Max Müller's words: "All created things perish". In Pali, sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā. Saṅkhārā means things that are put together, made of parts and causes.
Anicca means impermanent: they don't last. Verse two seventy-eight: "All created things are grief and pain". Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā.

Not that everything is miserable, but that nothing put together can give lasting satisfaction, because it's always slipping away. And verse two seventy-nine, in Müller's older English: "All forms are unreal".

The Pali is sabbe dhammā anattā: all things are not-self. Nothing, anywhere, is a fixed, permanent self to hold onto. Buddhists call these the three marks of existence: impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, not-self.
One small detail repays a close look. The first two verses say all saṅkhārā, all made things.
The third says all dhammā, all things whatsoever, a wider word, so that even nibbāna, which isn't made, is included in not-self.

And the Buddha's last words, in the long account of his final days, echo the first verse: all made things are subject to decay; strive on with diligence. It ends a week that kept pointing here. Make an island.
Little by little. Easy to see others. Wisdom can live in any body.
The practice makes it. Your feet make the journey.

how: Buddhist teachers across schools teach the three marks of existence, impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and not-self, and meditators often use verses 277–279 as reflections to return to.

o: everything made of parts and causes, which passes
everything God made at the start of the world
only living beings, the ones born and dying

games.q: match each Pali word to its meaning.

s: verse 278 means everything in life is miserable
it means nothing put together can give lasting satisfaction, because it keeps slipping away.
the third verse uses a wider word than the first two
all dhammā, all things, not just all saṅkhārā, made things.
the Buddha's last words echo verse 277
all made things are subject to decay; strive on with diligence.

games.q: you've just seen, really seen, that everything you own and love is changing and will pass. what do the verses say that seeing leads to?
o: turning from suffering: the way to purity.
games.why: each of the three verses ends almost the same way: the one who knows and sees this grows weary of suffering and turns from it; in verse 277, "this is the way to purity."

practice: Watch three things change: the breath, each one beginning and ending, no two the same; a sound, a car, a bird, a hum, arriving and fading; a thought, appearing, staying a moment, and dissolving on its own.
You don't have to make them pass; they already do. Just see it, and let the seeing be gentle.

wordCard.voice: All created things. Verses two seventy-seven to two seventy-nine: all made things pass, all are unsatisfying, all things are not-self; seeing this is the way to purity.

orig.note: Pali: something put together, a conditioned thing — sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, all made things pass.

carryVoice: Your line: all things pass. The good and the hard alike. That's a week, and day two hundred ten.
